newsitem.title: UK: Moody's - Major Hungarian banks' outlook positive.
newsitem.headline: Moody's - Major Hungarian banks' outlook positive.

text.p: Moody's rating agency said on Thursday that the credit outlook for major Hungarian banks was positive.
However, it said that although the situation was improving, Hungary's economic transformation to a market system was incomplete, and "further enterprise shake-out is likely".
In its first study of the country's banking system, Moody's said the banks operate in a tough economic environment that could impinge on their performance.
The report cited high inflation (with the CPI estimated at around 25 percent for 1996), along with high unemployment (Moody's forecasts a 10 percent rate this year).
The nation's large government fiscal deficits (forecast to be 7.4 percent of GDP in 1996) "could have growth ramifications if not controlled," the Moody's report says.
Nevertheless, it said the banks had made large strides in improving the capabilities they needed to meet these challenges.

Moody's said the Hungarian government "does have an interest in supporting the largest banks until the market system is well-established." That interest was reflected in the government's recent bank and debtor consolidation programmes that had helped to reduce the high levels of problem loans on the banks' books.

Currently, Moody's rates the deposits of five banks in Hungary, four at Ba2 (the sovereign ceiling for foreign currency deposits in Hungary), one a notch lower at Ba3. The bank's financial strength ratings range from D ("adequate") to E+ ("very weak intrinsic financial strength").

The report said that, given Hungary's high inflation rate, the banks' profitability was thin. In part this was due to the low level of lending caused by the transition to a market system and also due to "delayed consolidation" of the sector.
In addition, the Moody's analysts said overheads were high and the banking networks needed further rationalisation.

That rationalisation might best happen by way of more dynamic competition. But, although they have universal banking licences, the large banks had tended to remain specialised as they were under the old system. As a result, Hungary's banking system was still highly segmented, the report added.
Moody's said it expected Hungary's regulatory framework was likely to be enhanced by a new "Act on Financial Institutions," due to be enacted by the end of this year.
"The framework will likely be positive for the banks' credit strength, since it should provide for regulation of a wider range of financial services," the report said.
"It should require financial businesses other than credit institutions to acquire licences to operate, which would enhance the overall regulatory structure of the country's financial system."
